To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the resistance to mouse hepatitis in C3H mice is acquired during ontogeny.

1) The resistance of the host is genetically determined, 2) the resistance is expressed by the cells of the host, and 3) there is a progressive maturation of this resistance in the cells of the mouse.

(1) C3H mice develop resistance to mouse hepatitis virus with increasing age, and that this resistance is expressed in macrophages in vitro; (2) the resistance is not complete at birth, but is acquired by the macrophages during the first two weeks of life; and (3) the maturation of resistance to mouse hepatitis in vitro is modified by the number of cells in the culture and by the duration of the culture period before inoculation with virus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the resistance of macrophage populations to mouse hepatitis virus in vitro and in vivo.
the development of resistance of the mouse to infection with mouse hepatitis virus.
the study of the resistance of the C3H mouse to a strain of hepatitis virus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ontogeny of macrophage resistance to mouse hepatitis virus is a function of the age of the mouse, the time in culture, the number of explant cultures, the type of culture medium, and the number of cells in a given culture, and that these variables are interrelated.

the ontogeny of macrophage resistance to hepatitis virus in the C3h mouse progresses from delayed susceptibility at birth, to complete resistance at 16 days of age, and that it is a process that is not completed in vitro.

resistance to the hepatitis virus in the C3 mice is not an innate property of the cells, but rather a property which is acquired by the cells as they mature, and which may be lost if the cells are removed from their normal environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
resistance of macrophage cells to mouse hepatitis virus in vivo and in vitro is dependent on the age of the mice from which they were obtained and on the culture conditions.
the ontogeny of macrophage resistance to mouse hepatitis virus in vivo and in vitro parallels the resistance of the host to the disease.
the macrophage is the first and primary cell to become involved in mouse hepatitis virus infections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
macrophages derived from liver cultures of young mice were more susceptible to infection with MHV than were macrophages from older mice.
macrophages are important in the host defense response to viral infections.
the resistance of cells in the mouse to hepatitis virus increases during the first 16 days of life and is maintained throughout life.
